name: Maya Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate an underground scoop loader at Grey Lantern mine and lead the two-person loading crew. I have a two-year technical diploma and know the tunnel corners by the sound of the tyres. My partner and I have grown children and about four months of expenses saved. I use an AI app now and then to sort fault notes after another operator has checked it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a faster fault note is useful if it leaves the scoop loader and tunnel checks to us. I would still walk the machine before driving underground. A tidy note does not show a fresh scrape on the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shifts and pay look steady in this picture. Four months saved and a few nearby mines give us room, though I would not spend the cushion lightly. Retirement is close enough that I want to see the pension figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my loading shifts and check each tunnel bend as usual. I would ask for a pension statement this year and compare it with our monthly bills. I would use the fault app only when the original notes were available to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The bills are covered and the machine still needs a careful operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which scrape would concern you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A new mark at the narrow east corner means the scoop may have clipped the wall. I would stop and measure the clearance. A small scrape on a scoop loader can show where the next tunnel collision will happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a new app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the mine should pay for its own tools. I would try a tested feature if it solved a real problem. I do not buy gadgets for their own sake.

I would keep the **pre-start walk** before each underground load.
think: My **shifts and pay** look steady, with four months saved and some nearby jobs.
I want **pension figures** before choosing a retirement date.
do: **Keep** loading at Grey Lantern and checking tunnel bends.
**Request** a pension statement and compare it with monthly bills.
feel: **Calm** about household income and the current job.

steps.text: Keep loading Grey Lantern ore and checking tunnel bends
Request pension statement before choosing retirement date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say planning software may change the mine office first, while the scoop loader still needs hands. I would ask for a trial of any new loading schedule. Apprentices should ride with an experienced operator before targets rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could keep my wage while robots spread slowly, but I worry about a planner cutting the second person from our crew. My own role is strong, yet a smaller crew could make each tunnel run riskier. I would want proof before agreeing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the AI loading schedule from the dispatcher after it had run safely for a month. I would compare planned trips with our actual tunnel times for four weeks. If a second crew position vanished, I would take the safety record to the foreman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mainly about the other operator and the tight corners. My own income still seems likely to hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which trip takes longer than a schedule expects?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loaded return through the east corner when the floor is wet. A planner might count the empty trip instead. I would time both and show the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a one-person crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a real safety trial showed who checks the tunnel while I steer. I cannot watch the back of a scoop loader and the front corner at the same time. The apprentice learns by being there too.

say: I would ask for a **loading trial** before changing crew size or targets.
I would keep **apprentices** beside experienced operators in tight tunnels.
think: My **own wage** looks fairly safe while hands-on robots spread slowly.
Removing the **second operator** could make the tunnel route less safe.
do: **Learn** the AI loading schedule after dispatch has tested it for a month.
**Compare** planned and actual tunnel times and raise any lost crew post with the foreman.
feel: **Uneasy** for crew safety, while her own income looks stable.
S1.quote: I cannot watch the back of a scoop loader and the front corner at the same time.
fieldNote: She expects **office planning** to change before underground driving.
Her first new AI step is learning a **tested schedule** after dispatch uses it.
She connects apprentice time to **safety**, not a general dislike of tools.

steps.text: Learn AI loading schedule after dispatcher tests it one month
Keep second operator on tunnel route if safety trial requires one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the loading crew that full thinking AI by 2028 changes planning first, and capable scoop-loader robots follow around 2031. Grey Lantern might buy them. I would ask for the purchase dates and paid places in remote maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty when thinking AI arrives and sixty-three when capable robots appear. If the mine replaced our underground loaders quickly, I might lose wages before our pension was enough. Four months saved helps, but it is not years of income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would hold off buying the new family car and get our pension projection this month. I would keep loading after 2028 while the mine still used drivers. If Grey Lantern posted a paid remote-maintenance role and funded instruction, I would take the course without giving up my loader wage first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I have some room to plan, yet a lost wage at sixty-three is a real possibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take another mine job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call nearby mines and ask what equipment they planned to buy. A current opening could vanish by 2031. I would apply only if a real paid post appeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No regular support. They have their own families, and four months saved gives us time to find work. I would ask them for help in an emergency, but first I would look for a paid role.

say: I would distinguish **2028 planning AI** from capable scoop-loader robots around 2031.
I would ask for **purchase dates** and paid remote-maintenance places.
think: At **sixty-three**, robot loaders could end my wages before the pension covers us.
Four months saved buys time, but not **years of income**.
do: **Delay** the family car purchase and request a pension projection this month.

feel: **Anxious** about losing wages before retirement is funded.
S2.quote: Four months saved helps, but it is not years of income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years to thinking AI and about eight to capable scoop-loader robots gives the mine time to train operators properly. I would ask for a trial timetable and apprentice places. We should learn what happens in a real tunnel before changing shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-three at thinking AI in 2031 and about sixty-six when capable robots arrive in 2034. We might retire by then if the pension projections work. If not, paid remote checks could carry us a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request pension projections for ages sixty-five and sixty-seven and compare both with bills. I would take paid remote-loader instruction if Grey Lantern posted a real monitoring position and kept my wages through training. I would keep showing the apprentice the east corner while people still drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The longer warning lets me test both the job and retirement numbers without rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a tunnel trial have to prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot would have to stop before the wall at the east corner on wet ground. I would ride with the safety team and mark the stopping distance. A robot scoop-loader test in an empty yard would prove little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension figure is lower than expected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would work longer if Grey Lantern still had shifts. I would ask about monitoring work, but I would not pay for an empty certificate. My partner and I would decide with the real monthly number.

say: I would ask for a **tunnel trial timetable** before capable robots around 2034.
I would keep **apprentice places** while people still drive.
think: At about **sixty-six**, retirement may work if monthly pension income covers bills.
A paid **monitoring role** could extend wages if retirement falls short.
do: **Compare** pension projections for sixty-five and sixty-seven with bills.

**Keep** teaching the apprentice the east tunnel corner.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to test retirement and work routes.
S3.quote: A robot scoop-loader test in an empty yard would prove little.
fieldNote: She would be **sixty-three** in 2031 and about sixty-six when capable robots arrive.

steps.text: Compare pension projections at sixty-five and sixty-seven with bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade before thinking AI and about thirteen years before capable robots gives us time for a practical handover. I would keep teaching apprentices the tunnel. The mine should name when trials start and which jobs remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight in 2036 and about seventy-one when capable robots arrive in 2039. I expect retirement before then if our pension stays on track. Four months saved is helpful, but I would still check the monthly figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my loader shifts for now and ask for a pension update each year. I would take an apprentice through the east corner and show the wall marks. My partner and I would choose a retirement date after seeing the latest statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our own income path, with concern for younger operators. Thirteen years is plenty of warning if the mine uses it honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a robot trial make you retire early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not by itself. My partner and I would look at the pension and our plans for home first. I would not leave steady scoop-loader wages for a robot trial announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new operator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tunnel and listen to the machine before trusting a tidy plan. I would show the east corner, not just hand over a picture. A good apprentice needs time on the actual route.

say: I would ask for a **practical handover** before capable robots around 2039.
I would keep **apprentices** learning the tunnel while people drive.
think: At about **seventy-one**, retirement before capable robots seems likely if pension income holds.
Our **four-month cushion** helps, but monthly pension figures still decide.
do: **Keep** loading and take an apprentice through the east corner.
**Request** a yearly pension update before choosing a retirement date.
feel: **Calm** about her household income path, with concern for younger operators.
S4.quote: I would not leave steady scoop-loader wages for a robot trial announcement.
fieldNote: The **2039 robot date** falls near age seventy-one, after likely retirement if pension figures hold.
She keeps **hands-on apprenticeship** beside careful trial of proven technology.
Her decision rests on **monthly income**, not the excitement of a machine trial.

steps.text: Keep loading and teaching apprentice east tunnel corner

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable scoop-loader robots could arrive around 2031, before we know the pension will cover us. Paid remote-maintenance training tied to real posts would help. I would also want a trial in the wet tunnel.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who rides the route before a robot goes underground alone. I have seen a small scrape at Grey Lantern mine become a blocked tunnel. I would want the apprentice beside a real operator for that first lesson.

headlineQuote: I have seen a small scrape at Grey Lantern mine become a blocked tunnel.
portrait: Maya Torres is a **58-year-old** underground scoop-loader lead at Grey Lantern mine, with a diploma, grown children and four months saved.
She has **typical pay** and some nearby mine options, giving her room to test changes before retirement.
She uses AI **occasionally**, after colleagues test it, and wants apprentices learning inside real tunnels.
Fast robot availability makes her **anxious** about wages; a longer warning lets her compare pension income with bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because capable scoop-loader robots could arrive around 2031 before retirement is funded.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid remote-maintenance training** tied to real posts and a wet-tunnel trial would help her plan.
